target_customer: Semiconductor fabs buying spare parts and secondary market equipment; at launch, buyers and sellers of used semiconductor equipment
problem: Used semiconductor equipment and spare parts are sold through opaque brokers that hide the source and price and charge high fees. Asseta runs a transparent marketplace that quotes, invoices and manages orders.
business_model: marketplace take rate (5 to 10 percent fee at launch versus about 50 percent broker fees per TechCrunch 2014)
product_category: B2B marketplace for semiconductor equipment and spare parts

founders.name: Anton Brevde
prior_employers: a large used semiconductor equipment broker (unnamed in the YC launch post)
founders.background_notes: Per YC launch post and TechCrunch 2014 and 2015.

technical_complexity.rationale: A listing and quoting marketplace; the hard part was sourcing parts and supplier trust, not engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Supplier network and part history build up over time, but brokers and rivals can copy a listing site.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Brokers were fragmented and no source shows incumbents copying Asseta. Moov Technologies, a rival marketplace, was acquired by Axion in 2026, a separate company.

market_need_then: The YC launch post sized used semiconductor equipment at about 6 billion dollars in 2010 sales, with brokers hiding sources and prices; TechCrunch 2014 cites broker fees near 50 percent.

branding.domain_note: Uses asseta.com; acquisition history not found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Plain B2B; stresses that buyers and suppliers never see each other.

brand_strength.rationale: Only trademark records and the company site found; a 2025 unrelated Asseta AI company now shares the name and may cause confusion.

pivots.why: Equipment sales were too infrequent to sustain a marketplace; spare parts raised deals from a few per year to 20 to 40 a month (TechCrunch 2015-03-13).

outcome_analysis: Asseta launched in YC Summer 2013 as a used equipment marketplace led by founders from an equipment broker, raised 535 thousand dollars in 2014 and 1 million dollars in 2015, then pivoted to spare parts because equipment deals were too rare. The company site now claims over 30,000 part sales and 450,000 listings with a team of four, a durable niche business with no exit.
notes: Competitors left empty: the YC launch post and both TechCrunch articles describe hundreds of unnamed brokers and auctions; named rivals (Moov, SurplusGLOBAL, AET) come only from current CB Insights data. Dealroom and CB Insights give 1.56M to 1.65M total across rounds, aggregator figures not recorded as extra rounds; the 2015 round total is not stated in TechCrunch. Company site claims over 30,000 sales since 2014. Asseta AI (accounting, 2025) is a different company. Location differs by source (Newport Beach per YC and site).
